intro: Martha Argerich plays the Hungarian Rhapsody No. 6, S. 244/6. It opens with a march in D♭ major, continues with a quick dance and an ornamented slow song, and ends with octaves in both hands in B♭ major.

sections.label: A · March in D♭ major
sections.mNote: Steady bass chords under a melody that crosses the barlines.

sections.label: B · Presto dance in C♯ major
sections.mNote: D♭ major is respelt as C♯ major for the faster tune.

sections.label: C · Andante, B♭ minor song
sections.mNote: A slow piano melody with pauses and ornaments.

sections.label: D · Allegro, dance in B♭ major
sections.mNote: The tune is set over a regular rhythm in the bass.

sections.label: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
sections.mNote: The right hand repeats each note with its octave.

sections.label: Coda · Octaves in opposite directions
sections.mNote: Chromatic scales spread outwards to the final B♭ major chords.

relations.label: The quick dance repeats
relations.basis: The Presto dance is a repeated unit between the opening march and the Andante. Both excerpts fall within the 85–126 s Presto region rather than in the later octave variations. CENS diagonal mean 0.989, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 18.5 s (cache/form/liszt-hungarian-rhapsody-6.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, Tempo giusto, D♭ major
cues.text: The left hand plays steady chords in D♭ major. Above them, the melody crosses the barlines against the march’s two-beat metre. Liszt marked the opening Tempo giusto.
cues.evidence: The opening bass, metre and overlapping melody are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form. IMSLP confirms the opening marking and key: https://imslp.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No.6,_S.244/6_(Liszt,_Franz).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sources of the melodies
cues.text: Liszt wrote down the tune of the short second section in 1840, three years before it was published in a folk-song collection in 1843. The opening melody is known as Chlopiczky.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard identifies the first melody and dates Liszt’s notation of the second to 1840, before its 1843 publication: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.

cues.title: Publication of Rhapsodies III–XV, 1853
cues.text: Rhapsodies III to XV were all published in 1853. Liszt took their material from an earlier set of twenty-two Hungarian songs and rhapsodies, selecting thirteen pieces and reworking them. Only the first two rhapsodies were entirely new.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard’s notes for Hyperion CDA67418/9, on the Hungarian Rhapsodies III–XV: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9

cues.title: Presto in C♯ major
cues.text: After a cadenza played largely on the black keys, the Presto begins. D♭ major is now written as C♯ major, with the same pitches under different names. The tune becomes a quick dance, its steps much closer together.
cues.evidence: The cadenza, Presto heading and enharmonic change from D♭ to C♯ major are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Andante in B♭ minor
cues.text: After the quick dance, the Andante moves to B♭ minor. The piano’s melody is ornamented and broken by pauses, with each phrase lengthened in an improvisatory rhythm. A long cadenza leads into the finale.
cues.evidence: The Andante in B♭ minor, its improvisatory rhythm and concluding cadenza are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horváth’s song, printed 1813
cues.text: The slow tune is by Ádám Pálóczi Horváth and was printed in 1813. Liszt had already used it in his Rumanian Rhapsody.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard identifies Horváth, the 1813 publication and Liszt’s earlier use in the Rumanian Rhapsody: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.

cues.title: Allegro in B♭ major
cues.text: The Allegro stays in B♭ and moves from minor to major. A repeated quaver rhythm in the bass accompanies the fast tune above it. This is the friss, the fast dance that occupies the rest of the rhapsody.
cues.evidence: The Allegro in B♭ major and repeated quaver bass are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody in octaves, right hand
cues.text: The right hand plays the tune in octaves, in fast repeated notes. Each melodic note sounds at two pitches an octave apart. Beneath it the left hand keeps the dance rhythm.
cues.evidence: The finale’s semiquaver octave melody and repeated quaver accompaniment are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Source of the final dance tune
cues.text: The tune of the final fast dance appears in a handwritten collection of Hungarian themes, the Nagy potpourri, held in the Goethe-Schiller Archive. Liszt received it from János Liszt, a relation by marriage.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard’s notes for Hyperion CDA67418/9, on Rhapsody VI: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9

cues.title: Coda in B♭ major
cues.text: The hands play chromatic scales in octaves in contrary motion. The closing chords are in B♭ major, the key of the finale. The opening march was in D♭ major.
cues.evidence: The contrary-motion chromatic octaves and closing B♭-major chords are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Black-key cadenza into the Presto
transitions.to: B · Presto dance in C♯ major
transitions.how: A piano cadenza, written largely on the black keys, separates the march from the Presto. Liszt respells D♭ major as C♯ major, so the tonic pitch stays the same. The measured bass chords of the opening stop, and the quick dance begins.
transitions.evidence: The opening cadenza and the Presto’s C♯-major notation are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: From Presto to Andante
transitions.from: B · Presto dance in C♯ major
transitions.how: The Presto ends and the Andante begins in B♭ minor, the relative minor of the opening D♭ major. The piano drops the quick dance rhythm and plays a melody with pauses and ornaments, in a free, improvisatory rhythm.
transitions.evidence: The succession of Presto and Andante, their keys and the slow section’s improvisatory rhythm are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: From the cadenza to the B♭ major Allegro
transitions.to: D · Allegro, dance in B♭ major
transitions.how: The Andante ends with a long piano cadenza. The Allegro follows in B♭ major, changing the B♭ minor of the preceding section by replacing D♭ with D♮. Repeated quavers in the bass set a regular dance rhythm under the fast tune.
transitions.evidence: The slow section’s final cadenza and the Allegro’s B♭-major key and repeated bass rhythm are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: Finale tune doubled in octaves
transitions.from: D · Allegro, dance in B♭ major
transitions.to: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
transitions.how: In the B♭ major finale, Liszt doubles the tune in octaves and repeats its notes in semiquavers. Beneath it the left hand keeps up the quaver rhythm. The melody carries on through the right hand’s rapid jumps.
transitions.evidence: The finale’s octave melody and quaver bass are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: Contrary-motion octaves to the close
transitions.from: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
transitions.how: The closing piano runs turn into chromatic scales in octaves, with the hands moving in contrary motion. These scales lead to the final chords in B♭ major, the key of the dance.
transitions.evidence: The contrary-motion chromatic octave scales and B♭-major conclusion are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: Pianist whose playing drew orchestral sound from the keyboard, and who at the end of his life turned to sparse music at the piano.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces, and no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Liszt always counted Hungary as his homeland, though the languages he used most easily were German and French. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano, and Antonio Salieri taught him composition. In 1823 the family moved to Paris, where the Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. He continued his education with private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha.
